cards.title: Cloud Storage — Object Storage on GCP
cards.teaser: Cloud Storage is GCP's fully managed object storage service — the equivalent of Amazon S3. Every object lives inside a bucket, is addressed by a URL, and can range from a single byte to 5 TB. The service is global, durable, and strongly consistent.

runs.text: Cloud Storage stores arbitrary binary objects (blobs) rather than files or blocks. An object has three parts: a key (its name, which can contain slashes to simulate directories), a value (the raw bytes), and metadata (Content-Type, custom headers, and GCS-managed attributes).
Key concepts:

items.text: — the top-level container. Bucket names are globally unique across all GCP projects. A bucket has a location (region, dual-region, or multi-region), a default storage class, and IAM policies.
— immutable blob stored in a bucket. Overwriting an object replaces it atomically. If versioning is enabled, the old version is preserved.
— Cloud Storage provides strong global consistency for all operations: reads after writes, reads after deletes, and list operations. There is no eventual-consistency window to reason about.
— GCS targets 99.999999999% (eleven 9s) annual durability through redundant storage across multiple physical devices.

runs.text: Common CLI operations:

The newer gcloud storage commands (GA since 2023) offer significantly faster transfers than the legacy gsutil for large workloads via parallelism and sliced downloads. For new scripts, prefer gcloud storage over gsutil.

Cloud Storage is a giant key-value store in the cloud: you put files in (keyed by a name), get them back by name, and the service handles redundancy, durability, and global access. Think S3 but on Google's network.

cards.title: Storage Classes — Access Frequency vs Cost
cards.teaser: Cloud Storage offers four storage classes that trade retrieval cost for storage cost. The right class depends on how often data is accessed: Standard for hot data, Nearline for monthly access, Coldline for quarterly, Archive for annual.

runs.text: All four classes share the same API, the same eleven-nines durability, and the same latency on retrieval. The difference is purely economic: lower-frequency classes cost less per GB per month but charge a retrieval fee and enforce a minimum storage duration.

items.text: — highest storage cost, no retrieval fee, no minimum duration. Best for frequently accessed data (websites, streaming media, active datasets). Roughly $0.020/GB/month in us-central1.
— lower storage cost, small retrieval fee, 30-day minimum storage duration. Best for data accessed at most once a month (monthly backups, log archives). Roughly $0.010/GB/month.
— even lower storage cost, higher retrieval fee, 90-day minimum storage duration. Best for data accessed at most once a quarter (disaster recovery replicas). Roughly $0.004/GB/month.
— lowest storage cost, highest retrieval fee, 365-day minimum storage duration. Best for data rarely if ever accessed (regulatory retention, long-term audit logs). Roughly $0.0012/GB/month.

runs.text: Summary comparison:

items.text: Class | Min duration | Retrieval cost | Best for

runs.text: Storing data in Coldline or Archive and then reading it frequently will cost far more than Standard. Model your access patterns before choosing a class — retrieval fees stack up quickly on large datasets.

GCS storage classes are a sliding scale: the less you plan to access data, the cheaper it is to store — but the more you pay to get it back. Choose based on how often you will actually need to read the data.

cards.title: Object Lifecycle Policies — Automate Storage Class Transitions
cards.teaser: Lifecycle policies let Cloud Storage automatically transition objects to cheaper classes or delete them after a defined time, without any application code. They are the standard mechanism for cost-optimizing long-lived data.

runs.text: A lifecycle policy is a set of rules attached to a bucket. Each rule has a condition and an action. When an object matches the condition, the action is applied.
Common conditions:

items.text: — object is older than N days.
— object is currently in a specific class.
— N newer versions of the object exist (useful for pruning old versions when versioning is enabled).
— object was created before a specific date.

runs.text: Available actions:

items.text: — transition to Nearline, Coldline, or Archive.
— permanently remove the object (or a non-current version if versioning is enabled).

runs.text: Example lifecycle configuration (JSON, applied via
gcloud storage buckets update gs://my-bucket --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json

items.text: Transition to Nearline after 30 days, Coldline after 90 days, and delete after 365 days — a classic log-retention policy that minimizes storage costs automatically.

runs.text: Lifecycle transitions are not instantaneous — GCS processes them once per day. Objects meeting a condition today may not be transitioned until the following day. Factor this into cost projections.

A lifecycle policy is a set of rules that tells GCS: after X days, move this data to a cheaper tier; after Y days, delete it. It automates the cost management work you would otherwise have to do in application code.

cards.title: Object Versioning — Immutable History on Overwrite
cards.teaser: When versioning is enabled on a bucket, overwriting or deleting an object creates a non-current version rather than destroying data. Every version is addressable by its generation number, giving you a full, immutable audit trail.

runs.text: By default, writing a new object with the same name replaces the previous one permanently. With versioning enabled, the old object is retained as a non-current version — it is not visible in default bucket listings but is still readable and billable.
Key versioning concepts:

items.text: — each version of an object has a unique numeric generation. Access a specific version:
— deleting a versioned object inserts a delete marker as the live version. The previous versions are still present. To permanently delete all versions, delete each generation explicitly.
— copy a non-current version back to make it live:

Non-current versions incur storage charges at the same rate as live objects. Pair versioning with a lifecycle rule that deletes non-current versions older than N days to prevent unbounded cost growth.
Versioning is required for soft-delete recovery and for WORM compliance via retention policies. If you need accidental-deletion protection, enabling versioning is the first step.
With versioning on, GCS never truly overwrites or deletes an object — it keeps the old copy as a non-current version. You can always go back to any previous state using the generation number.

cards.title: Retention Policies — WORM Compliance Lock
cards.teaser: A retention policy on a bucket enforces a minimum retention duration on every object. Objects cannot be deleted or replaced until the retention period expires, satisfying write-once-read-many (WORM) compliance requirements.

runs.text: Retention policies are used when regulatory requirements (SEC 17a-4, HIPAA, FINRA) mandate that records are preserved and tamper-proof for a minimum period. They work at the bucket level and apply to all objects in the bucket.
How retention policies work:

items.text: in seconds, days, months, or years:

— once locked, the retention period can only be increased, never decreased or removed. This is the immutability guarantee required for compliance. Lock with:

runs.text: Before locking, a retention policy can be freely modified or removed. Locking is irreversible — it signals to auditors that the policy cannot be circumvented even by bucket owners.
Do not lock a retention policy unless you are certain of the required period. A locked 7-year policy on a test bucket that was accidentally given a retention policy will cost you 7 years of storage.
A retention policy says: no one can delete or overwrite these objects for N days, not even the bucket owner. Lock the policy and that promise becomes auditor-grade — even GCP cannot undo it.

cards.title: Bucket-Level vs Object-Level IAM
cards.teaser: Cloud Storage supports both bucket-level IAM (the modern default) and object-level ACLs (legacy). Uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs entirely, simplifying the permission model and eliminating the risk of ACL misconfiguration granting unintended public access.

runs.text: Cloud Storage has two access control mechanisms that can exist simultaneously on a bucket with legacy access:

items.text: — standard GCP IAM policies granting roles like
to principals at the bucket scope. IAM is the recommended model.

— legacy per-object or per-bucket Access Control Lists, inherited from Google Cloud Storage's earliest design. ACLs allow granting access to individual objects independently from the bucket's IAM policy.

runs.text: Uniform bucket-level access (UBL) disables ACLs entirely. All access is controlled exclusively through IAM. This is strongly recommended because:

items.text: Eliminates split-brain access control — you cannot have an object made public via an ACL that bypasses a restrictive bucket IAM policy.
Simplifies auditing — one IAM policy to review, not thousands of per-object ACLs.
Required for VPC Service Controls and Organizational Policies that restrict public access.

runs.text: Enable uniform bucket-level access:

New buckets created after May 2022 have uniform bucket-level access enabled by default. For existing buckets, you can enable it at any time — once enabled it cannot be disabled for 90 days (a protection against accidental access expansion).

Uniform bucket-level access means: forget per-object ACLs, use standard IAM for everything. It is simpler to audit and eliminates a class of misconfiguration where an individual object is accidentally made public.

cards.title: Signed URLs — Temporary Scoped Object Access
cards.teaser: Signed URLs grant time-limited access to a specific Cloud Storage object without requiring the caller to have a GCP IAM identity. Any HTTP client — browser, mobile app, curl — can read or write an object using nothing but the URL.

runs.text: A signed URL encodes the bucket, object name, allowed HTTP method (GET, PUT, DELETE), expiration time, and a cryptographic signature generated by a service account. Anyone who holds the URL can perform the specified action on the object until the URL expires.
Common use cases:

items.text: — generate a short-lived PUT signed URL server-side, return it to a browser or mobile app, and let the client upload directly to GCS without routing the file through your backend.
— serve private files to authenticated users with a GET signed URL that expires in minutes, preventing URL sharing from providing indefinite access.
— share a specific object with a partner who has no GCP account.

runs.text: Generate a signed URL (V4 signing, recommended):

The signature uses the credentials of the calling identity (user or service account). For server-side generation in application code, use the Cloud Storage client library with a service account key or Workload Identity.
Signed URLs bypass IAM entirely — anyone with the URL can access the object. Keep expiration windows short (minutes, not hours) and avoid logging URLs where they could be harvested.
A signed URL is a pre-authorized, expiring link to one specific GCS object. Hand it to anyone — no GCP account required — and they can read or write that object until the timer runs out.

cards.title: Cloud Storage FUSE — Buckets as a Filesystem
cards.teaser: Cloud Storage FUSE (gcsfuse) mounts a GCS bucket as a POSIX filesystem, allowing applications that expect local file paths to read and write Cloud Storage objects without code changes.

runs.text: gcsfuse is an open-source FUSE adapter that translates local filesystem calls into GCS API calls. Once mounted, a bucket appears as a regular directory — applications can use
open()
read()
write()
, and directory listings against it.
Mount a bucket:
Key use cases:

items.text: — Vertex AI and GKE workloads that need to read training datasets from GCS without modifying the training framework.
— apps that read/write local paths and cannot be refactored to use the GCS SDK.
— mount a bucket for ephemeral read access during a function invocation.

runs.text: Important limitations to understand:

items.text: Not a full POSIX filesystem — no hard links, no atomic rename across objects, no append-in-place.
Performance is network-bound — random read/write patterns that work well on local NVMe will be slow over gcsfuse.
Concurrency is GCS-level, not filesystem-level — no file locking semantics.

runs.text: GKE supports native Cloud Storage FUSE mounting via the GCS FUSE CSI driver, which avoids running gcsfuse as a sidecar. This is the recommended approach for Kubernetes workloads.

gcsfuse tricks your application into thinking a GCS bucket is a regular folder on disk. It is useful when you cannot change the code — but remember it is a cloud API underneath, not a local disk, so performance and semantics differ.

cards.title: Filestore — Managed NFS for GCP
cards.teaser: Filestore is GCP's fully managed NFS service. It provisions a dedicated NFS server that VMs, GKE pods, and Cloud Run jobs can mount as a shared filesystem — critical for workloads that require concurrent multi-writer file access.

runs.text: Cloud Storage and gcsfuse do not provide true concurrent write semantics. Filestore does. It is built on NFS v3 / NFS v4.1 and presents a fully POSIX-compliant shared filesystem that multiple clients can mount simultaneously with proper lock semantics.
Filestore tiers:

items.text: — 1 TB to 63.9 TB, up to 180 MB/s, 600 IOPS. Dev/test workloads.
— 2.5 TB to 63.9 TB, up to 480 MB/s, 60,000 IOPS. Production NFS with moderate performance.
— 10 TB to 100 TB, up to 25 GB/s throughput. Designed for large-scale, high-performance HPC and ML workloads.
— 1 TB to 10 TB, multi-zone redundancy, 99.99% SLA. Mission-critical shared filesystems.

runs.text: Create and mount a Filestore instance:

items.text: On the client: mount -t nfs -o rw,intr <IP>:/vol1 /mnt/nfs

runs.text: Filestore is the right choice when multiple VMs or GKE pods must read and write the same files concurrently — content management systems, shared build caches, EDA tools, and NFS-backed PersistentVolumeClaims in GKE.
Filestore is a managed NFS server in the cloud. Multiple machines can mount it at the same time and read or write files concurrently, with proper locking — something Cloud Storage simply cannot do.

cards.title: Persistent Disk — Block Storage for VMs
cards.teaser: Persistent Disk is GCP's network-attached block storage for Compute Engine VMs. It comes in four tiers — pd-standard, pd-balanced, pd-ssd, and pd-extreme — that trade IOPS and throughput for cost.

runs.text: Persistent Disk (PD) volumes are independent of the VM lifecycle: they persist when the VM is stopped or deleted, can be attached to multiple VMs simultaneously in read-only mode, and can be live-resized without downtime.
The four Persistent Disk tiers:

items.text: — rotational disk equivalent. ~0.75 IOPS/GB read, ~1.5 IOPS/GB write. Best for large sequential workloads (Hadoop, batch processing, cold data). Cheapest per GB.
— balanced price/performance. 6 IOPS/GB, same throughput as pd-ssd but lower max IOPS cap. The default choice for most workloads — boot disks, development VMs, moderate databases.
— higher IOPS (6 IOPS/GB, higher sustained limit than pd-balanced). Suited for latency-sensitive transactional databases, OLTP, and Kafka.
— provisioned IOPS up to 120,000 IOPS and 2,400 MB/s throughput per disk. Designed for the most demanding databases (Oracle, SAP HANA). IOPS are explicitly provisioned, not derived from disk size.
Tier | Media | IOPS model | Best for
pd-standard | HDD | Size-derived (~0.75/GB) | Batch, cold data
pd-balanced | SSD | Size-derived (6/GB) | General purpose, boot disks
pd-ssd | SSD | Size-derived (6/GB, higher cap) | Transactional DBs, Kafka
pd-extreme | SSD | Provisioned (up to 120k) | Oracle, SAP HANA, ultra-high IOPS

For pd-standard and pd-balanced, IOPS scale automatically with disk size — a 200 GB pd-standard gives 150 read IOPS. The only way to provision IOPS independently of disk size is pd-extreme (or Hyperdisk).

Persistent Disk is the hard drive for your GCP VM — but it lives on the network, not inside the machine. The four tiers go from cheap spinning-disk speeds up to provisioned SSD IOPS for the most demanding databases.

cards.title: Hyperdisk — Next-Gen Block Storage with Independent Scaling
cards.teaser: Hyperdisk is GCP's next-generation block storage that decouples capacity, IOPS, and throughput into three independently adjustable dimensions. You can scale any one without resizing the others — unlike Persistent Disk where IOPS are tied to disk size.

runs.text: With Persistent Disk, increasing IOPS means buying more capacity (IOPS are derived from GB). Hyperdisk breaks this coupling: you set capacity, IOPS, and throughput independently and can adjust them without detaching the disk from the VM.
Hyperdisk tiers:

items.text: — general-purpose; replaces pd-balanced for new workloads. Adjustable IOPS (up to 160,000) and throughput (up to 2,400 MB/s). Multi-writer support.
— maximum performance for mission-critical databases. Up to 350,000 IOPS and 5,000 MB/s throughput. Single-instance attach only.
— optimized for high-throughput, lower-IOPS workloads (streaming, analytics, large sequential reads). Up to 2,400 MB/s.
— designed for ML model serving; can be attached to up to 2,500 VMs simultaneously in read-only mode for fast, scalable model loading.

runs.text: Dynamic adjustment example — scale IOPS without resizing the disk:

Hyperdisk is the strategic direction for GCP block storage. For new production workloads, especially databases and analytics engines, Hyperdisk Balanced and Hyperdisk Extreme should be evaluated before defaulting to Persistent Disk.

Hyperdisk lets you say: I want exactly 50,000 IOPS and 500 GB of space, and scale either one independently later. With regular Persistent Disk you had to buy more space to get more IOPS — Hyperdisk removes that constraint.

cards.title: Storage Transfer Service — Bulk Data Migration
cards.teaser: Storage Transfer Service moves data into or between Cloud Storage buckets at scale — from AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, on-premises HDFS, or other GCS buckets. It handles scheduling, checksums, and deduplication automatically.

runs.text: Storage Transfer Service (STS) is designed for workloads where you need to move hundreds of TBs or PBs reliably, without managing the transfer infrastructure yourself.
Supported sources:

items.text: — direct cloud-to-cloud transfer over the public internet or AWS PrivateLink.
— migrate blobs with SAS token authentication.
— list of public URLs to ingest.
On-premises / other cloud (Transfer Service for On Premises Data)
— install an agent on the source machine; agents transfer data to GCS over the network.
— replicate between buckets, across regions, or to different projects. Also used for scheduled bucket synchronization.

runs.text: Create a transfer job via gcloud:

items.text: gcloud transfer jobs create s3://source-bucket gs://dest-bucket --source-creds-file=creds.json

runs.text: Key features:

items.text: — run once or on a recurring schedule (hourly, daily).
— include/exclude by prefix, suffix, or last-modified date.
— choose whether to overwrite existing objects and whether to delete objects from the source after transfer.

runs.text: For very large on-premises datasets (100+ TB) where network transfer would take weeks, consider Transfer Appliance — a physical rack-mountable device that GCP ships to your datacenter for offline bulk ingestion.

Storage Transfer Service is GCP's managed data mover — point it at S3, Azure Blob, or another GCS bucket, set a schedule, and it handles moving petabytes reliably with integrity checks. You do not manage the transfer infrastructure.

cards.title: CMEK — Customer-Managed Encryption Keys via Cloud KMS
cards.teaser: By default, GCP encrypts all data at rest using Google-managed keys. Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) let you provide your own key from Cloud KMS, giving you control over key rotation, auditing, and the ability to immediately revoke access to all encrypted data.

runs.text: GCP's default encryption (Google-managed keys) is transparent and automatic — every object in GCS, every Persistent Disk, every Hyperdisk is encrypted at rest with no configuration required. CMEK adds a layer where
your
key in Cloud KMS is used to wrap the data encryption key (DEK) before it is stored.
CMEK encryption model (envelope encryption):

items.text: GCS generates a unique Data Encryption Key (DEK) per object.
The DEK is encrypted (wrapped) using your Cloud KMS Key Encryption Key (KEK).
The wrapped DEK is stored alongside the object. The DEK plaintext never leaves GCP's memory.
To decrypt, GCS must call Cloud KMS to unwrap the DEK. If you revoke the KMS key's IAM permission, GCS cannot decrypt — access to all objects using that key is effectively cut off.

runs.text: Apply CMEK to a bucket (all new objects use the specified KMS key):
CMEK vs CSEK (Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys):

items.text: — your key lives in Cloud KMS, managed by GCP but owned by you. Integrates with IAM, audit logging, and automatic key rotation.
— you supply the raw AES-256 key bytes on every API call. GCP never stores the key. Higher operational burden; the key must be provided in every request header.

runs.text: Revoking a CMEK key does not immediately delete data — but it does make all data encrypted with that key permanently inaccessible. This is a powerful compliance control ("crypto-shredding") and an equally powerful accidental data-loss mechanism. Protect your KMS key IAM policies carefully.

CMEK means GCS still encrypts your data, but it has to ask your KMS key to unlock it every time. If you pull the key, the data is gone — not deleted, just permanently unreadable. That is the compliance guarantee.
